result.summary: Latium arms for war, and the river-god Tiber tells Æneas in a dream to seek Evander's Arcadians at Pallanteum. Evander welcomes him, tells of Hercules and Cacus, and offers Pallas and Etruscan allies. Venus gets arms from Vulcan, and Æneas receives a shield showing Rome's future history.

scenes.title: Latium Arms for War
scenes.summary: Turnus raises the war standard, Latin leaders muster forces, and Venulus is sent to Diomede. Æneas, watching, is tossed by anxious thoughts.
scenes.stakes: Æneas and the Trojans face a united Latium in war.

scenes.title: Tiber's Dream and the Voyage
scenes.summary: Tiber appears to Æneas, promises the omen of the white sow and advises an alliance with Evander. Æneas prays, sacrifices the sow to Juno, and rows upriver on calmed water.
scenes.stakes: Æneas risks defeat and the loss of his people's new home without allies.

scenes.title: Welcome at Pallanteum
scenes.summary: The Trojans reach Evander's city during a sacrifice to Hercules. Pallas challenges them; Æneas pleads kinship, and Evander recalls Anchises and welcomes them to the feast.
scenes.stakes: Æneas needs allies; rejection would leave the Trojans isolated.

scenes.title: Hercules and Cacus
scenes.summary: Evander tells how Hercules killed the fire-breathing monster Cacus, who stole his cattle. The Salii sing of Hercules' labours.
scenes.stakes: Cacus's victims and the herdsmen faced the monster's terror; Hercules risked fire and smoke.

scenes.title: Tour of Future Rome
scenes.summary: Evander walks Æneas through the site, recounting its early history under Saturn and pointing out future landmarks, then lodges him humbly.

scenes.title: Venus and Vulcan's Forge
scenes.summary: Venus persuades Vulcan to make arms for Æneas. Vulcan goes to the forge in Ætna's island and sets the Cyclops to work on a shield.
scenes.stakes: Venus fears for her son's life in the war.

scenes.title: Evander Offers Allies
scenes.summary: Evander proposes that Æneas lead the Etruscans against Mezentius and gives Pallas and horsemen. A sign from Venus confirms the call, and Æneas departs.
scenes.stakes: Æneas needs Etruscan allies against Turnus and Mezentius.

scenes.title: Evander's Farewell to Pallas
scenes.summary: Evander prays for his son's return, and the cavalry rides out to the Etruscan camp near Cære.
scenes.stakes: Evander may never see Pallas again.

scenes.title: The Shield of Æneas
scenes.summary: Venus presents Vulcan's arms. The shield shows Roman history from the wolf and Romulus to Actium and Augustus's triumph.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic of Hercules, from his grandfather Alcæus.
Another name for the smith god.
Epithet from the island Cythera, linked to her cult.

notable_quotes.reason: Evander urges Æneas to be worthy of a god by scorning wealth.
Closing line: Æneas shoulders the fame and fate of his descendants.

analysis.text: Book 8 links Æneas's struggle to Rome's future, with prophecy in the Tiber's omen, the site of Rome and the shield.
The shield glorifies Augustus and the victory at Actium, reflecting Virgil's Augustan setting.

legacy.text: The shield of Æneas became a model for ekphrasis, the poetic description of an artwork, after Homer's shield of Achilles.

fun_facts.text: Virgil's Cacus story gives an Italian setting to Hercules's cattle-driving from Geryon.

language_notes.text: Teucrians are the Trojans, named after their ancestor Teucer; Dardan likewise means Trojan, from Dardanus. The Latians are the Latins.
"Chief of Laomedon's line" means Æneas, a descendant of the Trojan king Laomedon.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy, used here for Troy itself.
The white sow and thirty piglets point to Alba Longa, "the White", founded thirty years later by Ascanius.
"Hesperian" means western, i.e. Italian; Hesperia is the Greek name for Italy, the western land.
Biremes are ships with two banks of oars.
"Immolates" means sacrifices; the sow is offered to Juno, as Tiber advised.
"Central cope of heaven" means the middle of the sky's vault: the sun is at noon.
Amphitryon's mighty child is Hercules, reputed son of Amphitryon (his real father being Jove). The "heavenly brotherhood" are the other gods honoured with him.
Evander is called Greek (Danaan) as an Arcadian; the two sons of Atreus are Agamemnon and Menelaus, leaders of the Greeks against Troy.
Dardanus, son of Jove and Electra, left Italy to found the Trojan line; hence Trojans are Dardanians, and Æneas claims kinship through Atlas.
Hesperia is the poetic name for Italy, "the western land"; the two seas are the Tyrrhenian above and Adriatic below.
"Gifts of the corn-goddess" means bread (Ceres, goddess of grain); "the wine-god" means wine (Bacchus). Both are metonymy for the substances.
Alcides is a name for Hercules, from his grandfather Alcaeus. Geryon was a three-bodied monster whose cattle Hercules took as one of his labours.
Amphitryon's son is Hercules, so called after his mortal stepfather. Jove was his true father.
Black choler is the old medical idea of bile, which was thought to cause anger.
Hero of Tiryns: Hercules was associated with Tiryns in Argolis, where he was raised or served Eurystheus.
Potitius and the Pinarian house were the two families said to hold Hercules' rites at Rome's Great Altar.
The Salii were Roman priests of Mars who danced and sang in procession. Here they are shown at Evander's rite.
The hymn lists Hercules' labours and feats: the centaurs Hylaeus and Pholus, the Cretan bull and the Nemean lion.
Typhoeus was a giant monster. Lerna's serpent is the many-headed Hydra that Hercules killed.
"Sprung from trunks of trees and hard oaken core" means early men were imagined as born from trees, a common ancient myth of primitive humanity.
Latium is explained by Latin latere, "to hide"; Saturn hid there after being driven from heaven by Jove.
"Hests" are commands or behests; the footnote marker [255] belongs to the edition.
The Asylum was a refuge Romulus later established for fugitives; the Lupercal was a cave sacred to Pan, called Lycæan from Arcadian Mount Lycæus.
The Capitol, later Rome's great temple hill, is named Tarpeian after the Tarpeian rock; Evander sees it still wooded, while the narrator knows its golden future.
The Ægis is Jove's storm-shield, shaken to raise tempests.
The cattle in the future Roman forum point to the later grandeur of the site, contrasted with its rustic state.
Alcides is Hercules, named after his grandfather Alcæus; he had visited Evander after killing the monster Cacus.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy, used here for the whole city. The Argive (Greek) kings destroyed it in the Trojan War.
The daughter of Nereus is Thetis, who got arms for Achilles from Vulcan; the spouse of Tithonus is Aurora (Dawn), who got arms for her son Memnon.
Electrum is a pale alloy of gold and silver, prized in ancient metalwork.
Pallas' slender craft means spinning and weaving, the arts of the goddess Pallas (Minerva).
The island is Vulcan's, in the Lipari group near Sicily. The Sicanians were an early people of Sicily; Æolian Lipari belongs to the wind-king Æolus' islands.
Chalybes were a people famed as ironworkers; their name here stands for smelted iron.
Cyclops: one-eyed giants who serve as Vulcan's smiths. Brontes means 'thunder' and Steropes 'lightning'.
Father of Lemnos is Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), whose cult centred on Lemnos; he is forging arms for Æneas at Venus's request.
Tyrrhenian means Etruscan; Tegea is a town in Arcadia, Evander's homeland, so the sword is a native Arcadian weapon.
Teucrians is another name for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.
Agylla is the old name of Caere in Etruria. The Etruscans were said to have come from Lydia in Asia Minor.
Mezentius's torture of binding living men to corpses is a famous example of his cruelty.
Mæonian is another name for Lydian, here meaning the Etruscans of Lydian descent.
Pallas's Sabine mother makes him half Italian, so by the soothsayer's decree he cannot lead the Etruscans.
Cythera's goddess is Venus, linked with the island of Cythera, near which she was said to have risen from the sea.
Venus had promised Æneas arms made by Vulcan, which she is now sending through the sky.
The Herculean fires refer to the rites for Hercules that Evander and Æneas had shared the day before.
Evander recalls a victory at Præneste, an old Latin town, when he was young and strong; he wishes Jupiter would restore that strength.
"Three lives" and a frame that could "thrice bear arms": Erulus had triple life and body, so he had to be killed three times.
Mezentius is the cruel Etruscan king, now Latin ally, whose war on Evander's people is the cause of this campaign.
"Care wears a double face" means anxiety is uncertain, pulling between hope and fear.
The "fallen lord" is Evander, who faints with grief and is carried indoors by his servants.
"Four-foot beat" imitates the galloping rhythm of Virgil's Latin line about hooves on the plain.
Pelasgians are an ancient pre-Greek people, here said to have settled early in Italy; Silvanus is a Roman god of woods and flocks.
Electrum is a pale alloy of gold and silver; cuishes are armor for the thighs.
The Sabine women were seized by Romulus's men at games, causing war with Tatius, king of the Sabine town Cures.
Mettus Fufetius, the Alban leader, broke faith with Rome's king Tullus and was punished by being torn apart by chariots.
Cocles (Horatius) held the bridge against Porsenna's army; Cloelia escaped captivity by swimming the Tiber.
The sacred geese of Juno's temple warned Manlius of the Gauls' night attack on the Capitol.
The Salii were dancing priests of Mars; the Luperci were priests who ran naked at the Lupercalia festival.
Catiline led a conspiracy against Rome in 63 BC; Cato was the strict Roman moralist, here lawgiver of the blessed.
The 'twin-born flames' on Augustus's brows are a radiant glow about his temples; the 'ancestral star' is the comet linked to Julius Cæsar.
Anubis, the dog-headed Egyptian god, stands for Egypt's strange gods set against Rome's Olympians.
Mulciber is another name for Vulcan; the listed peoples are far-flung nations of Africa, Asia and Europe.

context_notes.text: Mezentius was an Etruscan king driven out by his people for cruelty. He now fights for Turnus.
Diomede, the Greek hero of Troy, settled in southern Italy. The Latins hope he will join them against the Trojans.
Evander's Arcadian settlement on the Palatine hill was the site of later Rome.
Juno, hostile to the Trojans throughout the poem, is the divine force behind the war.
The site is the future Rome. Evander's small settlement on the Palatine hill is later the centre of the empire.
An olive branch was a sign of peace and a suppliant's token, offered to show friendly intent.
Mercury, son of Maia and Jove, was Evander's ancestor; Maia was one of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas.
Priam's sister Hesione had been carried off by Hercules and given to Telamon of Salamis after Laomedon's Troy was sacked.
Vulcan was the god of fire and the forge, which explains his son Cacus's fiery breath.
Juno hated Hercules as the son of her husband Jove by a mortal woman. She sent the serpents to his cradle.
Evander is an Arcadian exile who founded the small settlement Pallanteum on the future site of Rome.
Saturn, the Greek Cronos, was overthrown by his son Jove and fled to Italy; his reign was remembered as a golden age.
Carmentis was Evander's mother, a prophetess; the Carmental gate later stood at the foot of the Capitoline.
Janus and Saturn were old Italian gods; the Janiculum and the Saturnian settlement lay on opposite sides of the Tiber and the Capitol.
Æneas has just landed in Italy at Jove's bidding. The Rutulians are the people of Turnus, his chief enemy.
Vulcan is the smith god and husband of Venus. Here he excuses himself gently, saying he would have helped Troy had fate allowed.
The Ægis was Pallas' (Minerva's) protective breastplate, bearing the Gorgon Medusa's severed head.
Turnus is king of the Rutulians and Æneas's chief enemy; he shelters Mezentius.
Tarchon is an Etruscan leader who becomes Æneas's ally against Mezentius.
Laurentum was the chief city of King Latinus and the Latins, who are about to fight the Trojans.
Evander is the Arcadian king ruling the future site of Rome; Pallas, his son, leads his horsemen to aid Æneas.
Evander fears Pallas will die; his wish to die first is tragic anticipation of the war's course.
Tarchon is the Etruscan leader allied with Æneas against Mezentius; Tyrrhenians are Etruscans.
Vulcan, god of fire and the forge, made the arms at Venus's request for her son Æneas.
Actium (31 BC) was the sea battle where Octavian, later Augustus, defeated Antony and Cleopatra.
Agrippa was Augustus's admiral at Actium; the naval crown was awarded for sea victory.
Mavors is Mars, god of war; Bellona is a Roman war goddess, and Discord is war's personified companion.
Apollo had a temple at Actium and was credited with aiding Augustus.

literary_notes.text: Æneas's darting thoughts are compared to sunlight reflected off water in a bronze vessel, flickering around a room.
Tiber appears as an old man in a gray mantle with reeds in his hair, giving the river a human form and voice.
The calmed river shows divine favour for Æneas's mission.
The waters and the wood stand in wonder at the ships, as though they were amazed spectators.
The contrast between Evander's humble town and later Rome hints at the future greatness that is the poem's theme.
"That mighty name" stands for the fame of Troy and its heroes, which instantly impresses Pallas.
Æneas flatters Evander and weaves reasons of worth, oracles and ancestry into a careful appeal for alliance.
The golden bridles given long ago to Pallas symbolize the lasting bond between the houses, and may foreshadow Pallas's fate.
Fear is said to have winged his feet, turning terror into a source of speed.
Thrice repeated 'thrice' builds Hercules' mounting frustration before the final burst of force.
The opened cave is compared to the underworld laid bare, making the horror and the gods' hatred vivid.
The hymn turns to address Hercules directly, calling him down to his rites as if present.
Evander is shown as aged and gracious, a kindly guide, while Æneas' eager curiosity displays his openness to learning.
"Race of worse grain and duller hue" likens the decline of ages to inferior metals, echoing the golden age idea.
The awe felt at the Capitol hints at its future sacred importance in Rome.
Evander's call to scorn wealth and embrace poverty, modeled on Hercules, sets a moral contrast between simple virtue and later Roman splendor.
Night is pictured as a bird with dark wings, closing the scene with a quiet image.
Vulcan's sudden desire is compared to lightning running along a cloud, suited to the fire god.
Venus is shown as shrewd: her beauty is a deliberate art that wins her purpose.
Vulcan rising to work is likened to a poor spinning woman waking before dawn, bringing the divine down to humble domestic labour.
The thunderbolt's ingredients, frozen rain, cloud, flame and wind, give a vivid, elemental picture of divine craft.
Gasping bellows and hissing copper convey the sounds of the forge.
The narrator's comment 'so inventive is the lust of torture' makes the tyrant's cruelty more vivid and condemns him.
The thunder and trumpet-like sound in a clear sky is a divine sign that confirms the decision.
Æneas addresses the absent Turnus and the river Tiber, foreshadowing the bloody war ahead.
Fear 'treads on the heels of danger' and the war-god's features 'loom', making the women's dread almost physical.
Evander speaks to Jupiter and wishes for lost youth, making his anguish as a father vivid.
His dread of terrible tidings anticipates Pallas's death later in the war.
Pallas is compared to the morning-star rising from the ocean, showing his youthful radiance and promise, with a hint of brief brilliance.
Watching women, dust and gleaming bronze convey the departure from those left behind.
The dark, sacred, enclosed grove creates a hushed, reverent atmosphere before the allies meet.
The shield previews Rome's future, so Æneas carries unseen the whole destiny of his descendants.
The tender tableau of the wolf nursing the twins gives Rome's origin a gentle, vivid picture.
The narrator suddenly addresses Mettus, voicing moral condemnation of oath-breaking.
Ships are compared to uprooted islands and clashing hills, magnifying the battle's grandeur.
Vulcan, a god, carves Cleopatra's coming death into her face, so the artwork foretells her defeat.
Æneas 'heaves on his shoulder' the fame and fate of his descendants, as the shield becomes their weight.
